analytic.title: Real Time Spent on Real Time

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Worst-Case Execution-Time (WCET) Analysis is the first phase of Timing Analysis, which attempts to verify that a set of real-time tasks can be executed on an execution platform such that all tasks respect their deadlines. WCET analysis determines upper bounds on execution times, which are then passed on to a Schedulability Analysis, the second phase of Timing Analysis. This clean separation into the two phases holds for single-core execution platforms. Multi-core platforms require a more complex interaction between WCET analysis and schedulability analysis.

We have solved the WCET-analysis problem for single-core platforms. Key to our success was the use of Abstract Interpretation for the static analysis of the behavior of architectural components such as caches, pipelines, buses, and peripheries. The Program-Analyzer Generator (PAG), which is based on Abstract Interpretation, allowed us to quickly develop and experiment with abstract domains, to arrive at sound, precise, and scalable solutions.

div.head: A Relevant Problem and a Sound Solution
div.p: We have solved the problem to determine worst-case execution times (WCETs) for real-time programs to be executed on single-core execution platforms using sound methods. Soundness has always been a central requirement to our efforts. The application area, after all, is safetycritical, more specially time-critical embedded systems, and one doesn't want to see cars colliding with other cars or into obstacles, planes crashing, or ships sinking due to missed deadlines as part of debugging an embedded software.

Hence, the overall goal of our research was to develop a sound and efficient method that delivers precise run-time bounds. The efficiency obtained was decisive for the practicality of the technology. This combination of reliability, precision, and efficiency was not easily attainable.

We did not solve the halting problem; one typically assumes that programs under analysis terminate, and if not, our tool will discover that it is unable to derive bounds on iteration or recursion. The problem sound WCET analysis has to cope with is complexity, i.e. the size of the combined state space of program states and architectural states and the huge number of paths through this space. Abstraction of the architecture is key to any solution that will scale.

div.head: A Sequence of Interesting Research Problems
div.p: We started by analyzing cache behavior and found compact abstract cache domains with efficient update functions, representing the effect of memory blocks on abstract caches. Pipelines did not provide for compact abstract domains. So, we were forced to essentially collect sets of concrete pipeline states, resulting in a large effort. Later we came up with a pipeline design that provided for compact abstract domains and very efficient analysis at a tolerable loss in performance [1].

We did not import much. We used the Implicit Path Enumeration Technique (IPET) technique of Li and Malik [2] to determine longest paths and we modified Patrick and Radhia Cousot's interval analysis [3] to work on executable code and with machine arithmetic. All the rest we developed ourselves. This allows me to determine a halfway realistic estimation of the effort needed to develop a sound analysis technique for a non-trivial industrially-relevant problem. The net effort ranges between 15 and 20 person years.

div.head: Timing Predictability
div.p: Airbus, in a joint European project, offered us an architecture as a challenge for our WCET-analysis technique that had a cache with a rather weird replacement strategy, actually a cheap emulation of a random-replacement cache. We found that one could only analyze 1/4 of the cache capacity. This triggered the idea of doing research into the time predictability of architectures, which produced a lot of interesting results [4], [5]. I must confess, though, that this research did not have the expected impact on architectural research and practice. This might change as it becomes clear that some of the same architectural features ruining timing predictability also open the door for hardware security-attacks, as has been shown by the appearance of the Meltdown und Spectre attacks.

div.head: The State of Affairs
div.p: When we started, measurement was industrys doubtful best practice. Meanwhile our method realized in different aiT tools of Absint is widely accepted and used in the aviation and space industry outside of the USA and by several key players in the automotive industry. The technology has been instantiated for many processor architectures in combination with a large number of compilers. Note that the reconstruction of the control flow is compilerspecific. As processor architectures more than 10 different implementations of the PowerPCs ISA, the Infineon TriCore, ARM architectures, LEON 2 and LEON 3, V850E, M68020, C16x/ST10, HCS12, and others were covered.

aiT has been integrated into the tool chain of several model-based design tools, such as SCADE Suite,TargetLink, and ASCET. Such an integration offers back annotation of modeling input with WCET estimates. aiT has also been integrated with the schedulability tool SymTA/S.

Ironically enough, with the advent of multi-core architectures the complexity of the WCET-analysis task has increased so vastly that measurement currently again is industry's best practice, even though it is very difficult to perform and does not produce sound results. The problem is caused by the interference on shared resources of tasks running on different cores [6]. Again static analysis can help here by analyzing the amount of interference and estimating the effect of the interference on the execution time of the tasks. However, a sound and scalable WCET analysis for multi-core platforms has yet to be found.

div.head: The Full Story
div.p: The full story of the development is covered in [7], several of the engineering aspects in [8]. The crucial problem for the validation and certification of the WCET-analysis tool has been to convince oneself, the customers, and the certification authorities of the correctness of the abstract machine model, the core of our WCET analysis. This is done by trace validation as described in [9].

div.head: Acknowledgements
div.p: I have enjoyed the cooperation with a number of excellent doctoral students in solving the WCET problem, too many to list them all. Special thanks go to Christian Ferdinand, Stephan Thesing, Henrik Theiling, Florian Martin, and Michael Schmidt. In the research on timing predictability I enjoyed the cooperation with Jan Reineke, Sebastian Hahn, Daniel Grund, Reinhold Heckmann, and Lothar Thiele.
Funding in a sequence of projects has been obtained by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft and the European Commission.
